exoplanet_archive_host_coordinates.selection_caveat: The archive gives no orbit size for this planet, so the atlas keeps it at the host-star coordinates and draws no orbit and no separate marker.

exoplanet_archive_host_relative_orbit.position_epoch: Selected atlas UTC time, as the phase that an observer in the Solar System sees; light travel time is not removed

source.label: NASA Exoplanet Archive Planetary Systems Composite Parameters
source.release: Checked-in snapshot; see object provenance for the generation time

conventions.node: The archive gives no node angle. The line of nodes is put at 90 degrees to the line of sight and parallel to the ecliptic plane.
conventions.inclination: An inclination that is not measured or is only a limit is drawn as 90 degrees (edge-on).
conventions.shape: An eccentricity or argument of periastron that is absent or is only a limit gives a circle.
conventions.phase: Phase uncertainty in orbits is sqrt(sigma_T^2 + (N * sigma_P)^2) / P. Above 0.25 orbit, or with no usable timing, the atlas draws the orbit and no planet marker.

exoplanet_archive_host_relative_orbit.selection_caveat: Orbit size and timing come from the archive. The orbit direction around the line of sight is a display convention, not a measurement. Period and reference time come from one paper where the archive has such a row; mixed values carry a flag. Transit timing variations, the time system, and the argument-of-periastron convention of each paper can move the true phase.

tess_toi_coordinates.selection_caveat: Stars with a TESS planet candidate (TFOPWG disposition PC or APC) and a distance in the table. A candidate is not a confirmed planet: follow-up observations show that many candidates are false positives. A star that is also a confirmed-planet host keeps its confirmed-host record.

tess_toi_host_coordinates.selection_caveat: A planet candidate, not a confirmed planet. The table gives no period, or no usable star surface gravity and radius, so the atlas calculates no orbit size. It keeps the candidate at the host-star coordinates and draws no orbit and no separate marker.

tess_toi_host_relative_orbit.coordinate_frame: Host-star heliocentric ecliptic position plus a host-relative Kepler orbit offset

source.label: NASA Exoplanet Archive TESS Objects of Interest (TOI)
source.release: Checked-in snapshot; see object provenance for the generation time

conventions.orbit_size: The table gives no orbit size and no star mass. The atlas calculates the star mass from the surface gravity and the radius (M = g R^2 / G) and the orbit size from Kepler's third law with the period. A mass below 0.05 or above 5 solar masses, or with an uncertainty as large as the mass, gives no orbit.
conventions.node: The table gives no node angle. The line of nodes is put at 90 degrees to the line of sight and parallel to the ecliptic plane.
conventions.inclination: The table gives no inclination. A transit signal needs an orbit that is almost edge-on, so the orbit is drawn at 90 degrees.
conventions.shape: The table gives no eccentricity, so the orbit is a circle.
conventions.phase: Phase uncertainty in orbits is sqrt(sigma_T^2 + (N * sigma_P)^2) / P. Above 0.25 orbit, or with no usable timing, the atlas draws the orbit and no marker.

tess_toi_host_relative_orbit.selection_caveat: A planet candidate, not a confirmed planet: the transit signal can have a different cause, for example an eclipsing binary star. Period and transit time come from the TESS Objects of Interest table. The orbit size is an atlas calculation from the star surface gravity and radius, and its uncertainty is large. The orbit direction around the line of sight is a display convention, not a measurement.

catalog_sky_position_reference_shell.coordinate_frame: Catalog ICRS sky position transformed to heliocentric ecliptic Cartesian coordinates

source.label: Cosmic Atlas display convention (no distance measurement)

catalog_sky_position_reference_shell.selection_caveat: The object has no usable redshift or distance. It is drawn on a fixed 1e9 ly reference shell so the sky position remains visible; the shell radius is a display convention and is never a measurement.
